items.settingsPath: Undo the run.
items.name: Remove the startup app delay
items.desc: Windows holds startup apps back for about ten seconds after sign-in so the desktop appears first. This lets them start straight away.
items.riskNote: The desktop and taskbar may feel busier for the first few seconds after sign-in, because everything that starts with Windows now starts at once instead of after the shell has settled.

items.settingsPath: Settings > System > Display > Graphics > Default graphics settings, and turn hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling off - or undo the run, which puts back whatever the driver had chosen.
items.name: Hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling
items.desc: Moves the scheduling of GPU work from the CPU onto the graphics card. Windows already turns it on where the driver supports it, so on many machines this only makes that choice explicit. Takes effect after a restart.
items.riskNote: Offered only where a graphics adapter supports it. A small number of driver and capture-software combinations are unstable with it on. If anything misbehaves after the restart, turn it back off in Settings, System, Display, Graphics.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run. For a single game, the Compatibility tab of its .exe's Properties has its own Disable fullscreen optimizations box, which is the reliable switch.
symptoms: game bar overlay missing in game
items.name: Turn off fullscreen optimizations
items.desc: Asks fullscreen games to run truly exclusive instead of through the borderless-window path the compositor prefers.
items.riskNote: Exclusive fullscreen costs you the fast alt-tab and the overlays that draw over borderless windows - Game Bar, Discord, and some capture software. Whether these values still change anything on Windows 11 is disputed, and on many modern games it makes no measurable difference, so treat it as something to test rather than assume.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run.
items.name: Turn off power throttling
items.desc: Stops Windows itself slowing background processes to save power. Apps that ask for efficiency mode for themselves - browsers' background tabs, for one - still get it. Needs a restart.
items.riskNote: On a laptop this costs battery life, and that is the whole point of the feature - it is why background tabs and idle apps are cheap. Worth it on a desktop, questionable on anything with a battery.

items.settingsPath: Windows Security > Device security > Core isolation, and turn Memory integrity back on. A restart is needed.
items.name: Turn off Core Isolation
items.desc: Switches off memory integrity and asks Windows to stop virtualisation-based security. Where Windows Hello's enhanced sign-in security still uses VBS it keeps running, and so does its overhead. This is the single largest performance setting on the list, and the single largest security one.
items.riskNote: Memory integrity is what stops a malicious or vulnerable driver from injecting code into the kernel, and virtualisation-based security is what isolates credentials from the rest of the system. Turning them off measurably raises frame rates and lowers latency, and measurably lowers how hard this machine is to compromise. Only worth it if you know why you want it. Takes effect after a restart, and Windows Security will report your device as not meeting the standard for hardware security. VBS is not forced off where Windows Hello depends on it: doing that has locked people out of signing in.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run.
items.name: Turn off multi-plane overlay
items.desc: The standard fix for screen flicker, black flashes, and stuttering video on multi-monitor setups, particularly with mixed refresh rates. Needs a restart, and is only offered where a display actually uses overlays.
items.riskNote: Multi-plane overlay exists to let the display hardware compose video without waking the GPU, so turning it off costs a little power during video playback. Only worth doing if you are actually seeing flicker. Reports on 25H2 disagree - some find this value no longer does anything there, others that it still fixes flicker - and one reports it breaking G-Sync.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run.
items.name: Group services into fewer processes
items.desc: Windows gives most services their own svchost process on machines with more than 3.5 GB of memory. This raises that threshold to 2 TB, so services share processes again.
items.riskNote: Saves a few hundred megabytes of per-process overhead and costs you the isolation that came with it: one service crashing can now take its neighbors down, and Task Manager can no longer tell you which service is using the CPU. Takes effect after a restart.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run.
items.name: Turn off network throttling
items.desc: Windows caps non-multimedia network traffic while audio or video is playing, to protect playback. This removes the cap.
items.riskNote: A marginal tweak, honestly - Microsoft does not document this value, and the one careful measurement of it found that turning the cap off does not improve DPC latency and makes the network driver's noticeably worse. It only ever bites on a large transfer running at the same time as media playback, and on a slow machine it can make that playback stutter. Included because it is standard in every other tool of this kind. Lenovo Vantage's Smart Performance checks this value and may put it back.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run, or run fsutil behavior set disablelastaccess 2 from an administrator prompt, which is the system-managed default, and restart.
items.name: Stop updating last-access timestamps
items.desc: NTFS records when each file was last read - deferred, at most once an hour per file, but still a write. This turns that off. Needs a restart.
items.riskNote: Backup and audit tools that key off last-access time can no longer tell a file has been read. Almost nothing does; Windows itself has shipped with this off by default at various points.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run, or run fsutil 8dot3name set 2 from an administrator prompt, which is the per-volume default. Files created in the meantime keep having no short name.
items.name: Stop creating 8.3 short file names
items.desc: NTFS keeps a DOS-era PROGRA~1 name alongside every long file name. This stops creating new ones. Existing ones stay.
items.riskNote: A few very old installers and 16-bit tools resolve paths through the short name and will fail without it. Nothing written this century does.

items.settingsPath: Settings > System > Advanced > File Explorer, and turn Enable long paths off.
items.name: Allow file paths longer than 260 characters
items.desc: Lifts the MAX_PATH limit for programs that opt in - Node, Python, and most modern toolchains. File Explorer is not one of them, and Git needs its own git config --system core.longpaths true as well.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run, or delete MaintenanceDisabled under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\Maintenance. The Automatic Maintenance page in Control Panel has no switch for it.
items.name: Turn off Automatic Maintenance
items.desc: The nightly window in which Windows defragments, scans, and runs its own scheduled work, and wakes the machine to do it.
items.riskNote: Defender's scheduled scan, disk optimization, system diagnostics, and the registry's own scheduled backup all run inside this window. Turning it off does not stop real-time protection, but it does stop the scheduled scan, and drive optimization stops happening on its own. Better addressed by changing the maintenance time in Security and Maintenance than by switching it off.

items.settingsPath: Settings > System > Storage > Storage Sense, and turn it off.
items.name: Turn Storage Sense on
items.desc: Windows clears temporary files monthly and empties anything that has sat in the Recycle Bin for 30 days. Downloads are left alone. The one item here that keeps freeing space after the run finishes.

items.settingsPath: Control Panel > User Accounts > Change User Account Control settings, and move the slider back up.
items.name: Stop UAC asking for confirmation
items.desc: Administrators are elevated without a prompt and without the screen dimming. User Account Control itself stays on, so Store apps and app containers keep working.
items.riskNote: Every prompt you would have seen becomes a silent yes. Anything already running as your account can then elevate itself without you knowing, which is precisely what the prompt exists to prevent. The secure desktop - the dimming - is also what stops another program from clicking the prompt for you. This is a real reduction in security, not a cosmetic one.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run. EnableSmartScreen is a policy, so the switches under Windows Security > App and browser control > Reputation-based protection stay locked while it is in place.
items.name: Turn off SmartScreen
items.desc: Stops Windows, the Store, and Edge checking downloads and sites against Microsoft's reputation service.
items.riskNote: SmartScreen is the warning that appears before an unrecognized installer runs, and it is the layer that catches a great deal of commodity malware before Defender ever sees the file. It also sends a hash of what you download to Microsoft, which is why the option exists. Turning it off means unknown installers run with no warning at all.

items.settingsPath: Settings > Privacy and security > Device encryption, and turn it on.
items.name: Prevent automatic device encryption
items.desc: Stops Windows silently encrypting the system drive the first time you sign in with a Microsoft account, and escrowing the key there.
items.riskNote: Only does anything on a drive that is not encrypted yet - it prevents, it does not undo, which is why it is not offered on a machine whose system drive is already encrypted. Leaving the drive unencrypted means anyone who takes the disk out can read it.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run.
items.name: Keep the hardware clock in UTC
items.desc: For dual booting with Linux. Stops Windows and Linux disagreeing about the time by the size of your time zone offset every time you switch.
items.riskNote: Only correct if the other operating system also treats the hardware clock as UTC, which is the Linux default. On a Windows-only machine this does nothing useful and can confuse firmware clock settings.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run.
items.name: Detailed blue screen
items.desc: Adds the four bug-check parameters to the crash screen and drops the sad face where there is one. 24H2 and later already show the stop code and the failing driver on their black restart screen, so there this adds little.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run, which puts back each plan's own numbers. There is no page for it - Windows hides this setting from Power Options - so by hand it is powercfg /setacvalueindex <plan> SUB_NONE f15576e8-98b7-4186-b944-eafa664402d9 1 and /setdcvalueindex with 2 (Balanced's defaults), for each plan, then powercfg /setactive SCHEME_CURRENT.
symptoms: find my device out of date
items.name: Drop the network while asleep
items.desc: Stops the wireless card staying associated through Modern Standby, on every power plan, so the machine can reach its deepest idle state instead of waking to service background traffic. Only offered on machines that sleep with Modern Standby.
items.riskNote: Nothing arrives while the lid is shut: no mail, no Teams or Slack messages, no Find My Device location updates, and Wake-on-LAN stops working. Everything catches up within seconds of waking. The saving is real but very machine-dependent - a few hundred milliwatts, which is roughly the difference between losing 1.5% and 0.7% of a laptop battery per hour, and close to nothing on a machine that already reaches its deep idle state.

items.settingsPath: Control Panel > Power Options > Change plan settings > Change advanced power settings > Sleep > Allow wake timers, and set it back to Enable on each plan - or undo the run, which puts back each plan's own numbers.
symptoms: wakes from sleep on its own
items.name: Stop scheduled tasks waking the machine
items.desc: Clears wake timers on every power plan, so a scheduled task cannot wake the machine from sleep. On a machine that sleeps in S3 this is a common reason a laptop wakes in a bag and comes out warm; on Modern Standby it is more often activity during standby, which this does not touch.
items.riskNote: Anything that relied on waking the machine to run stops happening while it is asleep - overnight backups, scheduled maintenance, and Windows Update installing on its own. Those all run at the next opportunity while the machine is awake instead, so nothing is lost, but nothing happens on a schedule either. An alarm set in an app will not wake the machine.

items.settingsPath: Control Panel > Power Options > Change advanced power settings, then set USB settings > USB selective suspend to Disabled and PCI Express > Link State Power Management to Off, on each plan - or undo the run, which puts back each plan's own numbers.
items.name: Let idle USB and PCIe devices power down
items.desc: Turns on USB selective suspend and sets PCI Express link power management to maximum savings, on every power plan, so idle peripherals and buses drop to a low-power state instead of being held awake. Link power management only takes effect where the firmware hands it to Windows.
items.riskNote: This is the pair most likely to be worth undoing. USB audio interfaces, some docks, and a few external drives handle being suspended badly and come back with dropouts, disconnects, or a device that needs replugging - and the symptom appears minutes later, nowhere near this setting. Some manufacturers ship selective suspend off on purpose for exactly that reason. The saving is small and steady rather than large. If anything on USB misbehaves after a run, this is the first item to put back.

items.settingsPath: Delete PlatformAoAcOverride from HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Power and restart. Undoing the run does the same. If the machine will not wake after this, hold the power button to force it off, start it again, and undo the run.
items.name: Use real sleep instead of Modern Standby
items.desc: Turns off Modern Standby so the machine uses S3 suspend-to-RAM: the CPU is genuinely off rather than idling, which is by far the largest sleep saving available. Needs a restart.
items.riskNote: The biggest saving here and the one most likely to go wrong. Modern Standby machines are shipped and tested by their manufacturer with S3 disabled in firmware. Where the firmware has no S3 at all, the machine is left with no sleep state - Sleep disappears from the power menu - and where it implements S3 badly the result is a machine that sleeps and will not wake, recoverable only by forcing it off and undoing the run. Instant-on goes away and resume takes a second or two. Try it on a machine you can afford to have to hard-reset, and undo it if sleep stops working. Only offered on machines that sleep with Modern Standby.
